title: C1: Challenge: What substitution does to the free variables
title_html: C1: Challenge: What substitution does to the free variables
html:
Let φ be a formula, x a variable and t a term, with t free for x in φ, and with x free in φ.

  1. Prove that the free variables of φ[t/x] are the free variables of φ other than x, together with the variables of t: FV(φ[t/x])=(FV(φ)∖{x})∪Var(t), with the notation of B2. Prove it in the following form, by structural induction on φ: for every φ in which t is free for x, if x∈FV(φ), then FV(φ[t/x])=(FV(φ)∖{x})∪Var(t); if x∉FV(φ), then φ[t/x]=φ. The term version, the atomic case and the connective cases are done below; prove the case of ∀yφ (the case of ∃yφ is the same).
  2. Show, with the capture example ∃y(y>x), t=y+1, that the conclusion can fail when t is not free for x. Show also, with an example of your own, that it can fail when x is not free in φ.

Given for (a). Terms. Let s be a term in which x occurs. Then Var(s[t/x])=(Var(s)∖{x})∪Var(t). By induction on s: if s is the variable x, then s[t/x]=t and both sides are Var(t). (A constant, or a variable other than x, does not contain x.) If s=f(s1,…,sn), then s[t/x]=f(s1[t/x],…,sn[t/x]); for each si containing x, the induction hypothesis gives Var(si[t/x])=(Var(si)∖{x})∪Var(t), and for each si not containing x, si[t/x]=si (as in the proof of the claim in the text). At least one si contains x, so the union over i is (Var(s)∖{x})∪Var(t).

Formulas. We prove, by structural induction on φ, the statement S(φ): if t is free for x in φ, then FV(φ[t/x])=(FV(φ)∖{x})∪Var(t) when x∈FV(φ), and φ[t/x]=φ when x∉FV(φ). The second half is the claim proved in the text, for every φ; so in each case below we assume x∈FV(φ) and prove the equation. Write E(χ) for the set (FV(χ)∖{x})∪Var(t).

Atomic. Let φ=R(s1,…,sn) with x occurring in some si. By the clause for atomic formulas, FV(φ[t/x]) is the union over i of the sets Var(si[t/x]). Exactly as in the term case for f(s1,…,sn) (the result for terms for each si containing x, si[t/x]=si for the others, and at least one si containing x), this union is E(φ). The same for s1=s2. (⊥ has no free variables.)

Negation. FV((¬φ)[t/x])=FV(φ[t/x])=E(φ)=E(¬φ), by the induction hypothesis (t is free for x in φ, and x is free in φ).

Binary connective. Let x be free in (φ∘ψ); then t is free for x in both parts, and x is free in at least one. If it is free in both, the induction hypothesis gives E(φ)∪E(ψ)=E((φ∘ψ)). If it is free in φ only, then ψ[t/x]=ψ, and E(φ)∪FV(ψ)=E((φ∘ψ)), because x∉FV(ψ). Symmetrically if it is free in ψ only.
